Chip pipeline02 / 25 · Part I · Materials

Czochralski crystal puller

Growing the crystal

A chip starts as one perfect crystal of silicon. In a Czochralski puller, 140 kg of ultra-pure polysilicon is melted in a quartz crucible, a small seed crystal is dipped into the melt, and the seed is turned and drawn slowly upward so the melt freezes onto it atom by atom in the same crystal order. Press Play to watch one run, from melting to lifting out a 300 mm crystal.

What happens

  1. Melt. Chunks of polysilicon and a measured pinch of dopant (boron for p-type) are melted in the quartz crucible by a graphite heater, under argon. Silicon melts at 1414 °C.
  2. Dip the seed. A seed crystal 8–20 mm across, cut along the chosen crystal direction, is lowered on a cable, warmed above the melt, and touched to its surface.
  3. Dash neck. The touch shocks the seed and creates dislocations. Pulling fast makes a thin neck 3–5 mm across, and the dislocations run out of its sides, so what grows below is dislocation-free.
  4. Shoulder. The pull slows down, so the crystal grows outward as well as down. It widens in a rounded crown from the thin neck to the full 300 mm.
  5. Body. Most of the run is spent here. The diameter is held at 300 mm by adjusting heater power and pull speed while a camera watches the bright ring where crystal meets melt. Crystal and crucible turn in opposite directions, and the crucible rises so the melt surface stays at the same height. Argon flows down past the crystal and out over the melt, sweeping away the silicon monoxide that evaporates from it, and leaves through exhaust ports in the chamber floor.
  6. Tail. At the end the crystal is pulled faster so it narrows to a cone. Lifting a full-width crystal off the melt would shock it and send dislocations back up the body.
  7. Cool and remove. The crystal is lifted into the pull chamber, the gate valve closes, and it cools before it is taken out and sent to be ground, sliced and polished into wafers.

Key numbers

Melting point of silicon1414 °C
Charge in a 24-inch hot zone140 kg24-inch crucible, the run drawn here; by 2002 most 300 mm crystals already came from 32-inch hot zones
Neck diameter3–5 mmDash necking; the seed itself is 8–20 mm
Rotationcrystal 5–14 rpm · crucible 6–12 rpmin opposite directions
One metre of 300 mm body≈ 165 kgderived from silicon's density, 2.329 g/cm³
A run5–7 daysper pulling run at Siltronic Freiberg, for 300 mm crystals larger than the 140 kg Tu et al. run drawn here

Why it matters

  • Dash necking (1959) is why crystals can be grown dislocation-free at all. Nearly every crystal grown for chips today still starts with a thin Dash neck (neck-free seeding exists but is rare).
  • Oxygen from the quartz crucible dissolves into the melt and ends up in the crystal. A little is useful, since it traps metal impurities, but it must be controlled. A magnetic field across the melt (MCZ) damps the convection that carries it; horizontal fields of 0.2 T and more are used. One horizontal-field process grows crystals below 5×10¹⁷ oxygen atoms/cm³, and the cusp field drawn here holds it in a set range along the length.
  • The ratio of pull speed to the temperature gradient at the growth surface decides whether leftover vacancies or extra atoms freeze into the crystal. Holding it at a critical value over the whole wafer grows near-perfect silicon with almost no voids, which the finest transistors need.
  • Bigger crystals mean bigger wafers and cheaper chips: a 300 mm wafer has 2.25 times the area of a 200 mm one. A 24-inch puller such as the EKZ 3500 holds crystals up to 2.5 m long and weighs about 9 tonnes.
